text: nature plants Circular RNAs derived from MIR156D promote rice heading by repressing transcription elongation of pri-miR156d through R-loop formation 5 1,6, Yong Yi1,6, Shengchao Ge 1,6, Zi Wang1, Zhangyu Wei1, 3, Haifeng Wang2, Yangwen Qian4, 1 & Yunfeng Liu In angiosperms, microRNA156 (miR156) acts as an intrinsic, endogenous developmental timer for the age-dependent transition from the juvenile to the adult phase1–3. However, the mechanisms modulating the age-dependent expression pattern of miR156 are still poorly understood4. In this Article, we report that circular RNAs (ciMIR156Ds) derived from pri-miR156d negatively regulate miR156 levels in an aging-dependent manner in rice. The ciMIR156D levels increase as plants age, which is inversely correlated with the changes of pri-miR156d and miR156 abundance. Consistent with this observation, ciMIR156Ds deficiency caused by a spontaneous mutation increases pri-miR156d and miR156 levels, resulting in a delayed heading phenotype, whereas ciMIR156Ds overexpression has opposite effects, demonstrating that ciMIR156Ds are negative regulators of miR156. We further show that ciMIR156Ds form R-loops with MIR156D at the region where they derive in an aging-dependent manner, which reduces the occupancy of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase II at that location and hence impedes pri-miR156d elongation. These findings reveal a mechanism for regulating heading date Flowering timing or heading date stands as a pivotal agronomic trait in rice cultivation, representing a critical transition from vegetative to reproductive growth.

text: It determines the production cycle, geographic and seasonal adaptability of rice5–7. Agronomic yield traits such as spikelet number, grain yield per panicle and seed set are also associated with rice heading characteristics7. Therefore, the mechanisms regulating heading date hold notable importance in improving rice variety traits and enhancing yield potential. Aging is one of the crucial factors determining flowering time8, serving as an endogenous signal to suppress flowering during the juvenile phase while ensuring flowering during the adult phase without reliance on exogenous inductive factors9. text: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are a class of non-coding RNAs containing the closed-loop structure. In animals, circRNAs play critical roles in regulating diverse biological processes via various functional mechanisms by interacting with proteins, RNAs and DNAs14. CircRNAs are also widely present in plants15,16. However, their functions remain to be investigated. text: To support this notion, we expressed a mutated copy of MIR156D harbouring the 133-bp deletion (miR156sdh) and a WT copy of MIR156D (miR156SDH) driven by its native promoter in Nip. Expression of miR156sdh, but not miR156SDH, increased accumulation of pri-miR156 and mature miR156 (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 3b), resulting in developmental defects similar to those of NIL-sdh (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). In addition, we expressed an miR156 short tandem target mimic (STTM156) driven by the MIR156D promoter (Extended Data Fig. 3e) in NIL-sdh. Expression of STTM156 restored mature miR156 levels and rescued the developmental defects of NIL-sdh, when compared with Nip (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 3c,d,f). Furthermore, overexpression of MIR156D under the control of the 35S promoter dramatically delayed the heading date and increased tiller numbers in Nip (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). Taken together, these results demonstrate that the 133-bp deletion increases miR156 levels, resulting in the developmental defects of sdh. text: LBA1 (At5g47010) required for NMD26,27 and found that pri-miR156d and miR156 accumulation was not altered in this mutant relative to WT (Extended Data Fig. 7). Next, we asked how ciMIR156Ds repress miR156d levels. They could not function as an miRNA sponge because of the lack of a miR156 binding site or act on pri-miR156d RNA since they are derived from the same strand and do not have predicted complementary binding regions. Previous 712 reports have shown that certain nuclear-localized circRNAs can alter the expression of their parent genes28,29. Because ciMIR156Ds are also localized in the cell nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 8a), we reasoned that they might affect pri-miR156d transcription. On the basis of the observation that some circRNAs bind their cognate DNA to form a RNA–DNA hybrid or R-loop to modulate gene expression30, we next asked if ciMIR156Ds could form an R-loop with their cognate DNA. Indeed, the R-loops in the region spanning the second intron to third exon of MIR156D were found in data generated by rice DNA–RNA immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (DRIP–seq)31 (Fig. 3a). Thus, we used dot blot with R-loop-specific antibodies to test if ciMIR156Ds could form R-loops in vitro. Incubation of R-loop free genomic DNA with ciMIR156D-1, ciMIR156D-2, ciMIR156D-3 and the positive control AtSEPs exon 5 circRNA30, but not the negative control circRNA5g05160 (ref. 22), generated signals (Fig. 3b). These signals were R-loop specific because they became undetectable after treatments with DNase I, which degrades DNA, or RNase H, which degrades RNA in RNA–DNA hybrids. Moreover, treatment with RNase R, which removes linear RNAs, showed that 49.8%, 45.5% and 34.7% of the total R-loop signal were generated by ciMIR156D-1, ciMIR156D-2 and ciMIR156D-3, respectively (Fig. 3b), suggesting that ciMIR156D-1 and ciMIR156D-2 exhibited a strong ability to form R-loops with their cognate DNAs, while ciMIR156D-3, which contains only the third exon, showed a weaker binding capacity. Notably, incubation of ciMIR156Ds with R-loop-free DNAs from sdh, which still contain substantial sequences complementary to ciMIR156Ds, did not generate R-loop signals (Fig. 3c), suggesting that the 133-bp deletion in sdh is crucial for R-loop formation. Supporting this result, ciMIR156D-3, which partially overlaps with the deleted region, formed a weaker R-loop with wild-type genomic DNA (Fig. 3b,c). Taken together, these results demonstrate that that ciMIR156Ds form R-loops with the DNA regions where they derive. Next, we used DRIP with antibodies recognizing RNA–DNA hybrids followed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) to validate in vivo ciMI156D-mediated R-loop formation in the second and fifth leaves. DRIP detected the enrichment of a circRNA–DNA R-loop in the region spanning both second intron and third exon of MIR156D in Nip but not in sdh (Fig. 3d,e). Moreover, the R-loop signals were higher in the fifth leaf than in the second leaf, which is consistent with the elevated ciMIR156D levels in respective leaves (Fig. 3d,e). Together with the in vitro results, these data reveal that ciMIR156D-1 and -2 form an R-loop with their cognate DNA in vivo. Next, we asked how the R-loop formed by ciMIR156Ds modulates pri-miR156 transcription. In plants, R-loops formed by circRNA–DNA pairing have been shown to modulate epigenetic modifications31,32. However, sdh did not substantially alter the levels of histone methylation or acetylation in either the miR156d coding region or the proximal region (Extended Data Fig. 8b,c). R-loops formed in gene bodies also can restrain RNA polymerase II (Pol II) extension rate during the elongation33. Indeed, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) data of Pol II showed that Pol II occupancy at the R-loop region of mature leaves (flag leaves)34, which had high ciMIR156D levels, was higher than that in ciMIR156D-low young leaves (seedling leaves) (Fig. 3a), suggesting that ciMIR156Ds may affect pri-miR156d elongation.
title: Circular RNAs derived from MIR156D promote rice heading by repressing transcription elongation of pri-miR156d through R-loop formation

text: To support this, we compared the Pol II occupancy at the MIR156D gene region in Nip and NIL-sdh in leaves of different stages. In the R-loop-rich fifth leaf (Fig. 3e), Pol II showed notably higher occupancy at the R-loop region in NIL-sdh relative to NIP (Fig. 3g). In contrast, in the R-loop-limited second leaf (Fig. 3d), the difference of Pol II occupancy between Nip and NIL-sdh was not substantial (Fig. 3f). These results reveal that ciMIR156D-1 and -2 affect pri-miR156d elongation in an R-loop-dependent manner. As the major contributor for miR156 production (Extended Data Fig. 9) in rice, the fluctuation of miR156d transcripts shall substantially impact on the miR156 level. In this study, we identified ciMIR156Ds derived from pri-miR156d as key regulators of heading date in rice. Two out of three ciMIR156Ds bind their cognate DNA locus, forming R-loops. The R-loops slow the transcriptional elongation of pri-miR156d, ultimately resulting in reduced accumulation of miR156. Notably, ciMIR156D levels increase from the first to fifth leaves, enabling them to modulate miR156 levels in an aging-dependent way. Indeed, lack of ciMIR156Ds causes delayed head date while overexpression of ciMIR156D results in earlier flowering time. How the ciMIR156D levels are modulated in an aging-dependent manner remains to be investigated. Intriguingly, circRNAs derived from MIR156 locus are also present in Arabidopsis and overlap with the R-loop at the region (Extended Data Fig. 10 and Supplementary Data 2), indicating that circRNA-mediated modulation of miR156 maybe a conserved mechanism to control the transition from the vegetative to reproductive stages. It has been reported that R-loops, formed near the transcription start site region of MIRNAs, promote cotranscriptional pri-miRNA processing35. This raised a possibility that R-loops formed by ciMIR156s may affect pri-miR156d processing, in addition to their role in transcription regulation. However, these R-loops were formed after pre-miR156d. Thus, their effect on pri-miRNA156d processing remains to be investigated. Multiple circRNAs have been shown to function through R-loop formation30,36, suggesting that they may extensively affect gene transcription through mediating R-loop formation. In agreement with this, we identified 460 circRNAs originating from 175 miRNA loci from rice circRNA database23 (Supplementary Data 3). Among them, 165 circRNAs from 78 miRNA loci potentially overlap with R-loops (Supplementary Data 4), suggesting that circRNA-mediated R-loop formation maybe a common mechanism in regulating miRNA levels.

Using >3,000 BC3F2 plants, the SDH locus was mapped to a region between markers RM555 and RM5869 on chromosome 2, and further narrowed to an ~85.8-kb region flanked by markers RM12584 and RM1259. text: The 2,423-bp promoter of MIR156D was cloned into pRHE vector by in-fusion cloning to generate the pRHE-pro156d construct. The genomic region of MIR156D from first exon to fifth exon was amplified from DNA of Nip or NIL-sdh and fused with the sixth exon using fusion PCR to obtain the miR156dSDH or miR156sdh fragments, respectively. The miR156dSDH and miR156sdh were cloned into pRHE-pro156d, to generate pRHE-Pro156d::miR156SDH and pRHE-pro156d::miR156sdh, respectively. The STTM targeting miR156 was amplified using PCR and cloned into pRHE-pro156d. The genomic region of MIR156D from first exon to fifth exon was mutated by site-directed mutagenesis and was cloned into pRHV under the control of the ubiquitin promoter to generate ciMIR156D overexpression construct.

text: RNA blot was performed as described in ref. 25. Briefly, after treatment with DNase I, 30 μg of total RNAs from various rice materials were separated by electrophoresis on 20% denaturing polyacrylamide gels, 713 transferred to a Hybond-N+ nylon membrane (Amersham Bioscience, GE Healthcare) and ultraviolet-crosslinked. After hybridization at 42 °C in ULTRAhyb-oligo hybridization buffer (Ambion) with a biotin-labelled (Invitrogen) probe, the membranes were washed twice at 40 °C in 2× SSC buffer and 0.5% SDS buffer for 30 min and for further biotin detection. Total RNA was extracted using the TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) from sequentially developed leaves (first to fifth leaves) or flag leaf of 5-week-old rice.

text: In vitro RNA transcription, circularization and purification were performed as described in ref. 37 with slight modifications. A total of 1 μg of PCR-amplified DNA fragments with T7 promoter were incubated with 2 μl of T7 RNA polymerase enzyme (Promega), 0.5 mM dNTPs, RNase inhibitor and 2 mM GMP to produce linear RNAs. After DNase I treatment, 50 μg of in vitro transcribed RNAs were incubated with T4 RNA ligase 2 (NEB) for in vitro circularization. Following elimination of linear RNAs with RNase R digestion, the resulting cirRNAs were purified with phenol–chloroform extraction and precipitated with ethanol. The purified circRNA was validated by PCR with divergent primers listed in Supplementary Data 5.

text: The divergent and convergent primers were designed for corresponding circRNA sequences and BSJ sites. After reverse transcription using random primers, controls were amplified using complementary templates generated from linear RNA with convergent primers and divergent primers were used to detect the circRNAs. PCR products were dissected from gel and purified using the gel extraction kit (Tiangen DP209) for sequencing. The accumulations of the ciMIR156Ds in total RNA of the fourth leaf of Nip were measured by droplet digital PCR using automatic digital PCR system DQ24 (Sniper).

text: DRIP assay was carried out as described in ref. 32 with slight modifications. The nuclei isolated from rice leaves were used to extract genomic DNA through three rounds of phenol, phenol–chloroform and chloroform extraction followed by cold ethanol precipitation. Purified genomic DNA was sonicated into fragments of 100–300 bp. The 3-μg fragmented DNA was kept as inputs and 5-μg fragmented DNA with or without RNase H treatment was purified and incubated overnight at 4 °C with S9.6 antibody (1:200, Abcam ab234957) in IP buffer (10 mM NaPO4, 140 mM NaCl, 0.05% Triton X-100) followed by incubation with 50 μl of protein A/G dynabeads). After washing with IP buffer three times, the beads were eluted with 300 μl of elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 10 mM EDTA buffer, 0.5% SDS) twice at 65 °C for 30 min. The S9.6 antibody-bound DNA was then purified using phenol–chloroform extraction and pelleted with ethanol. DNA was resuspended for PCR assay. The percentage of immunoprecipitated DNA was calculated as fold-change over the input.

text: The histone methylation and acetylation assays were carried out as described in ref. 38 with slight modifications. Briefly, 1 g of the rice material was crosslinked in 1% formaldehyde. Then, nuclei were isolated and resuspended in nuclear lysis buffer. Following this step, DNA was interrupted with ultrasonic crusher and diluted with fivefold ChIP dilution buffer. After prehybridization the protein A/G dynabeads, antibodies recognizing H3K27ac (1:500, Abcam ab4729) or H3K27me3 (1:500, Abcam ab6002) were used for immunoprecipitation at 4 °C. After washing, DNAs were eluted, subjected to decrosslink and purified with phenol–chloroform extraction. The resulting DNAs were then precipitated with isoamyl alcohol and resuspended for PCR assay.

text: Equal amount of in vitro synthesized circRNAs were incubated with the DNA template respectively, heated for 5 min at 65 °C in hybridization buffer (10 mM pH 7.5 Tris-HCl, 0.1 mM EDTA, varying NaCl concentrations) and slowly cooled down to room temperature for R-loop formation in vitro. Then 2 μl of reaction solution was spotted onto Hybond-N+ nylon membrane. After air-drying, the membrane was preblocked in 5% milk overnight at 4 °C and then incubated with S9.6 monoclonal antibody (1:1,000, Abcam ab234957), followed by incubation with goat anti-mouse-HRP secondary antibody (1:10,000, Abcam ab205719) to detect DNA–RNA hybrids loop. DNase I, RNase H and RNase R (NEB) treatments were performed according to manufacturer’s instruction using a standard hybridization buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 50 mM NaCl, 0.1 mM EDTA)30. DNase I digests double-stranded DNA; the endoribonuclease RNase H degrades RNA in the RNA–DNA hybrids; the exoribonuclease RNase R degrades linear RNA, but not circular RNA.

text: The cirRNA data of rice downloaded from Plantcircbase (v.7.0, http:// ibi.zju.edu.cn/plantcircbase/index.php)23 and BEDTools (v.2.28.0, https://bedtools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html)39 were used to identify circRNAs located within a 2-kb range upstream and downstream of miRNAs. A total of 460 circRNAs were identified in this process. Subsequently, based on previously published rice R-loops peak data31, BEDTools were used to identify circRNAs that may potentially form R-loops with at least a 1-bp overlap between circRNA and R-loop peak, resulting in the identification of 165 circRNAs originating from 78 miRNAs, which may mediate R-loop formation.
